newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Southpower wants to bring in domestic competition.
newsitem.headline: Southpower wants to bring in domestic competition.

text.p: Power companies want to bring competition to domestic power consumers, but metering problems are holding them back, Southpower strategic business development manager Graham Hodge told the New Zealand Press Association.

He said risk was crippling the retailing industry if they proceeded with new metering technologies without first agreeing how to handle the millions of transactions potentially involved, "The movers and shakers want to see competition advanced," he told NZPA.

A number of power companies are trying out new metering systems in an effort to bring real-time power pricing -- wholesale electricity prices move half-hourly -- to domestic customers. With that in place power companies could then compete with each other for domestic customers.
Hodge said metering technology was no longer the primary obstacle to real domestic competition.
What the industry had to agree on, he said, was a way of reconciling the half-hourly power consumption of an energy trader's customers against the prices being paid on the wholesale market.

The power industry already has a metering and reconciliation agreement for settling sales of power in other company's networks. But with a potential market of one million odd-homes, and 48 half-hour periods a day to price, Hodge said the industry had to find a way to avoid a costly "wash-up process" -- the settlement of actual power used and its offer price, against the wholesale price and the cost of delivered energy at the customer's door when it was used.
"Wash-ups could be a downstream rolling problem which we believe will be a very expensive for the back office parts of the industry to keep track of."
Palmerston North-based power company Electro Power this week launched its metering service which it said had enabled some households to cut their power bills by 30 percent.

Gisborne-based Eastland Energy has been working with a British company developing a remote real-time meter reading system, while Dunedin Electricity is trying out a system known as profile metering. Rather than recording actual consumption half-hourly, a meter is loaded with a deemed demand pattern based on location, history, size of household, and bills accordingly.
Hodge said that so long as meters had scope for two-way communication between a customer and a supplier, the choice of technology was not really an issue.

Consumers might ultimately be able to buy their own meters from a range available, but with about $100 invested in each existing household meter, it was important that the next generation of meters did not close out future options.
"Before we go racing off installing meters out there we need to ask ourselves whether these things have the features to support an industry of the type we think we may be operating in future."

The system Electro power has developed with Auckland technology company Spectral and New Zealand Insurance not only offers consumers greater control of their power purchases, but also offers a home security package that uses the power lines to raise an alarm in a nominated home or with a security company.
The key-pad operated system has scope for reading gas and water meters also present in the house and has capacity to communicate with smart'' appliances as they are developed.

Hodge said it was a misnomer to call the new technology a metering system. Future systems may, based on a households' recorded power use pattern, go as far as remotely selecting daily an energy supplier from a range of electronic offers.

With the development of micro-generation technology, "meters" might also be required to log when it is cheaper to buy energy on market and switch off a site's generation, or alternatively, when to offer that generation into the town power network.
While the margins on energy trading were small, Mr Hodge said all suppliers would try to offer a bundle of services to generate greater value and maintain their residential business.

But with control of consumption data effectively moving from the power companies' billing systems to the new smart meters in the home, that business would become truly contestable and power suppliers would have to drive costs out of their residential supply business.
Hodge said one scenario was that the industry may ultimately form one neutral metering company from their existing billing systems.
